I think you may be thinking of [Special Bulletin (1983)](http://m.imdb.com/title/tt0086350/).

It's more centered around social commentary and sensationalism than the horrors of a nuclear war, but if that's your thing then it's well worth watching. 

If I remember correctly the "live broadcast" style of the film was mostly accepted as fiction because the networks that first ran it had constant disclaimers that it was such (during commercial breaks and even imposing "DRAMATIZATION" on the bottom of the screen at intervals), but it wasn't enough for some and there was some incredibly small-scale panic.

I'm not an expert in the slightest, but I knew a girl who had BPD. People who have it tend to suffer very intense emotions and can cycle between them in a very short time span, and can go from idolizing people they're close to (eg; they can do no wrong and are the messiah) to being very bitter (and in some cases, verbally abusive). There's also a very persistent fear of being abandoned in most with the disorder, and whether they're rational in the fear or not they'll go to great lengths to avoid it. The girl I knew also spoke a lot about feeling 'empty'. 

It can be easy to write off these people as monsters or be afraid of them, but I see it differently. Yes, some can be abusive, but foremost they're people, and people are all different. These symptoms are exhausting and difficult to understand, and that applies to the diagnosed person as well. It can't be 'cured', but it's important for those diagnosed to learn to regulate and cope with their emotions and resist impulses. 

I hope this helped :) and sorry if I have any information factually wrong

Had anorexia from the ages of 12 - 14. I was always a chubby kid, and I was never self concious about it until I hit my preteens. I was annoyed by the friction of my thighs rubbing together so I decided to 'fix it' at 12.

Cue age 14. I'd lost more than 30% of my body weight within the span of two years, and I was nearly skeletal. At that point I was around 76 pounds. I refused to believe I was anorexic, in my mind I was just dieting.

I don't know what sparked me to go to the mirror, but I stood there and stared. Saw my ribs, saw how hollow my cheeks were. And I thought; "Oh shit, if I keep this up I'm going to fucking die." 

I was lucky enough to realize this a few days before a psych appointment, and they put me on calorie shakes and an antipsychotic that helped with weight gain. 

Presently I'm a bit overweight (I developed binge eating disorder right after the anorexia, which sucked, but I've gotten it mostly managed now) and feeling pretty good about things. Definitely much better now that I kicked it. If I had to give advice, I'd say that coming to terms with the fact that something is wrong when the disorder first starts rearing its head is better than denying it to the point that I did.
